Hook: In 2025 the world bought about ninety-one million new vehicles. Here is what the companies that make them kept of each dollar of revenue, the year before and that year. Toyota kept 7.6 cents, down from almost ten. Volkswagen, 2.1. General Motors, 1.5. And three of the best-known names in the business lost money: Honda, Ford, and Stellantis, the maker of Jeep, Fiat and Peugeot, which lost 14.5 cents on every dollar it took in. The car is the most desired consumer product of the last hundred years. Why is it so hard to make money making it?

Mass production of cars began in one building. On the first of April, 1913, at Ford's Highland Park plant in Michigan, a line of workers began assembling the flywheel magneto, a small part of the Model T's ignition, each one sliding along from one worker to the next. One worker had needed about twenty minutes to build one; on the line it took 5. Henry Ford wrote that the idea came from the overhead trolleys of the Chicago meat packers. Then the whole car. Standing still, a team needed twelve hours and twenty-eight minutes to assemble a chassis. Pulled by a rope and a windlass down a line two hundred and fifty feet long, past piles of parts, with six assemblers walking alongside: five hours and fifty minutes. On a raised moving line in 1914: one hour and thirty-three minutes. Mass production had begun.

The second arrival came from Japan. Toyota's roots are in looms. In 1896 Sakichi Toyoda built a power loom that stopped itself when a thread broke, so that no bad cloth was made and no one had to stand watching the machine. Toyota calls the idea jidoka: automation with a human touch. His son Kiichiro, who started the car company, put the other idea this way: 'A complete car cannot be built if even one part is missing... without this control, we could have a mountain of parts and still not be able to build a car.' Make only what is needed, when it is needed: just in time. After the war Taiichi Ohno, backed by Eiji Toyoda, built the two ideas into the Toyota Production System, with its little cards, called kanban, that tell each step only what the step after it has used. Carmakers everywhere later set out to copy it.

And now a third arrival. In 2015, fewer than one new car in a hundred sold in the world ran on a battery. In 2025, 25 in a hundred did, counting plug-in hybrids. And China, which in 2015 exported 4 billion dollars' worth of cars, exported 110 billion in 2025, more by value than Japan. This film follows the money through the business, from the plant to the dealer to the loan, and asks where it goes, and why so little of it stays with the people who make the car.
Industry, Built. Part seventeen: automobiles. Why is it so hard to make money making the most desired product of the century?
Run: Chapter one. Run it. You make a car; the orders are coming in below plan; your rival has the same problem. Hold the price, or pay a discount?

You run a plant that builds one crossover. It sells to dealers at 45,000 dollars. The parts, materials, freight and warranty on each one cost 36,000, so each car leaves 9,000 dollars to pay for everything else. Everything else is large and does not shrink with the orders. Two shifts of workers, each costing about 288 million dollars a year, paid whether the line is busy or not; the tooling, the engineering of the model and the plant's overhead, another 900 million. So the plant must sell 164,000 cars a year, 66 per cent of what it can build, just to break even. The plan was 220,000.

This line is your plant's profit for each number of cars it sells. At the plan, 220,000 cars, it makes about 504 million dollars. Then the first months of orders come in, and they are thirty per cent below plan: 154,000 cars a year. At that rate the plant loses 90 million. And across the aisle, in the same showrooms, your rival's model, built in a plant just like yours, is selling just as slowly. Buyers compare the two closely. A discount on yours would take buyers from the rival, and a discount on theirs would take them from you.

So here is the choice, for you and for the rival, set out as a table. Your profit is in blue, the rival's in orange. If you both hold the price, you each lose 90 million. Pause, and choose. Suppose you discount by 3,000 dollars and the rival holds. The rival's buyers come to you; you sell almost all the plant can build and make 22 million, while the rival loses 560. Suppose the rival discounts and you hold: the mirror image, and you are the one losing 560 million. And if you both discount, neither takes the other's buyers, the market grows only a little, and you each lose 486 million. Look at your own choice column by column. If the rival holds, you do better discounting. If the rival discounts, you also do better discounting. The rival reasons the same way. Both discount, and both end up far worse off than if both had held. Economists call it the prisoner's dilemma, and the car business lives in it.

There is a third move that the table left out. If both of you cut a shift and hold the price, you each build only 125,000 cars a year, but you stop paying a crew to stand idle, and each loses 63 million: the least bad outcome on offer. It is sometimes called capacity discipline. It is hard to keep. Cutting a shift means lay-offs, suppliers left idle and a smaller share of the market, and each maker would rather the other one cut first. That is the first answer to this film's question: the plants cost the same whether they are full or not, so every maker is tempted to fill its own, and when they all try, prices fall for everyone. Keep that in mind; it comes back in China.
Making: Chapter two. How a car is made: what happens between a coil of steel and a car on a truck?

Toyota describes its plants in five steps, the same steps most car plants follow. Coils of sheet steel arrive and huge presses stamp them into the panels of a body: doors, roof, sides, floor. Robots weld the panels into a shell, called the body in white because it is still bare metal. The shell is dipped and sprayed in coat after coat of paint. Then final assembly: the engine or the battery, the wiring, the dashboard, the seats, the glass, the wheels. Toyota counts some 30,000 parts in a car, many of them made by other companies. Last, every car is checked, driven off the line and loaded for the dealers.

How much work goes into one? America's census of businesses counts it. In 2022 170 companies ran 210 plants that assemble cars and light trucks. They employed 213,363 people and shipped 357 billion dollars' worth of vehicles. Those plants put together about 9.7 million vehicles that year. If each person worked about two thousand hours, that is roughly 44 hours of work for each vehicle: a rough figure, since not everyone in those plants works on the line. The model plant of the Run it game, with two shifts of two thousand people, comes to about 29 hours a car, and finishes one about every minute. Roughly one person's working week, for a machine of thirty thousand parts. That is what a century of the moving line bought.
Dollar: Chapter three. Where a car's dollar goes. Of the price of a new car, who gets what?

Take the average new car that AutoNation, one of America's largest car retailers, sold in 2025: 52,075 dollars. The dealer kept about 5 cents in the dollar as gross margin on the car itself; we will see later where the dealer really makes its money. The rest went to the carmaker. And here is the surprise. For every dollar of cars the assembly plants shipped, they had paid about 76 cents to other companies, for parts and materials. Their own payroll was about 4.7 cents. What is left has to pay for designing the car, tooling the plant, the warranty, the marketing and the head office, with profit last. In 2025 General Motors' North American business kept 6.8 cents of each dollar of revenue as operating profit, and the petrol side of Ford, 3.0. A carmaker is, more than anything, a buyer and an assembler of other companies' work.

What do they buy? The census asked the assembly plants. The biggest single item is metal stampings, 44 billion dollars' worth: the panels and brackets other companies press. Then transmissions and the parts that carry power to the wheels, then engines, other parts, seats and interiors, electrical and electronic equipment, glass, plastics. Near the bottom, almost a rounding error at 2.9 billion dollars: semiconductors. Remember that line. In all the plants bought 271 billion dollars of materials and parts that year. Every one of those suppliers wants a margin too, which is the squeeze a carmaker lives in.
Scale: Chapter four. Scale and platforms. Why does a carmaker need to build millions of cars?

A car has to be designed, tested, crash-tested and certified before the first one is sold, and the bill for that is the same whether the maker then sells ten thousand or ten million. Here is each maker's research and development spending in its latest year, divided by the vehicles it sold. The dashed lines are what one and ten billion dollars a year come to per car. Toyota spread its engineering over more than nine million vehicles: about 971 dollars a car. GM, Volkswagen, BYD and Ford, one to three thousand. Tesla, 3,909, since its research includes its work on self-driving and robots. Then the newcomers. Rivian spent 39,482 dollars of research for each of the 42,247 vehicles it delivered; Lucid, 76,472 for each of 15,841. Only Ferrari spends like that and does well: its revenue comes to about 524,000 euros for every car it ships.

Now divide each company's net profit by the vehicles it sold. The volume makers earn hundreds of dollars a car, or a few thousand: Toyota about 2,681, Tesla 2,313, BYD and Volkswagen under a thousand, GM 436; Ford lost 1,858. Rivian lost 86,302 dollars on every vehicle it delivered, and Lucid 170,321. And Ferrari made 132,366 on each car. Two ways to live in this business: sell millions of cars at a thin margin, or a few thousand at a fat one. In between, the bill for engineering and tooling eats you.

So carmakers share the engineering. A platform is the part of a car that buyers never see: the floor, the structure that protects them in a crash, the wiring, the electronics. Suppose a new one costs 6 billion dollars to engineer and lasts 6 years. Built under one model selling two hundred thousand a year, it costs 5,000 dollars a car. Put five models on it, a million a year, and it costs 1,000. This is why car companies merge. In 2021 Fiat Chrysler and France's PSA became one company, Stellantis, with more than a dozen brands to spread across fewer platforms. It is also why a newcomer with one model finds the arithmetic so hard.
Plant: Chapter five. The plant's break-even. How full must a car plant be to make money?

Go back to the plant from the Run it game and ask a plainer question: how full must it be? Here is its profit at every level of output. Below about 66 per cent of what its two shifts can build, it loses money, because the crews, the tooling and the engineering cost the same at any level. Above it, every extra car adds its full margin, and profit climbs steeply. A car plant is a machine for turning volume into profit, and its owner lives on the steep part of this line. Carmakers say so themselves. Toyota told its investors in 2026 that its break-even volume had risen significantly, because of new investment and America's tariffs.

How full are real plants? The Federal Reserve has measured America's motor vehicle and parts plants against their capacity every month since 1948. On average they have run at about 77 per cent. In bad years the line falls off a cliff: 51 per cent in 1982, 44 per cent in 2009, the year Chrysler's business was sold in a government-sponsored restructuring, and in April 2020, with the plants shut for the pandemic, 14 per cent. In 2025 the plants ran at about 65 per cent: about the break-even of the model plant.

Now look at the newcomers. Rivian's plant in Normal, Illinois, can build 215,000 vehicles a year. In 2025 it built 42,284: about a fifth. Lucid's plant in Arizona has room for 90,000; it built 18,378. Rivian's annual report puts the consequence plainly: running below capacity makes the cost of each vehicle much higher than it would be if the plant were full. That is where the losses per car of the last chapter come from.

The same arithmetic makes every launch lopsided. Plan the model plant for two hundred and twenty thousand cars a year. If the orders come in as planned, it makes about 504 million dollars. If they come in thirty per cent short, it loses 90 million: 594 million worse than plan. If they come in thirty per cent above plan, it makes only 270 million more, because two shifts cannot build more than two hundred and fifty thousand cars, and a third crew would cost more than the extra cars earn. The bad surprises cost more than the good ones pay. That is the second answer to the film's question.
Lean: Chapter six. Lean production. Why did the whole industry copy Toyota, and what did it bet?

Here is what Toyota changed. In a push system each step works as fast as it can and hands its output on. When one step is slower, or a part is faulty, the work piles up in front of it: inventory, which costs money, takes space, and hides mistakes, because a bad batch can sit unnoticed in a pile. In Toyota's pull system, nothing moves until the step after asks for it. The card, the kanban, travels backwards: the assembly line uses a box of parts, the card goes back, and only then is another box made. Almost no piles, and a problem shows itself at once, because the line stops. Kiichiro Toyoda's warning was that a maker can have a mountain of parts and still not be able to build a car. Lean production, as it came to be called, set out to have neither the mountain nor the missing part.

Lean production was a bet that stock is waste. But stock is also a cushion. This line is the cars sitting on America's dealer lots, measured in months of sales. For years it ran at about two and a half months, 2.25 in 2019. In the crash of 2009 it shot up to 4.6 months: cars nobody was buying. Then 2021. Factories could not get enough chips, and by January 2022 the lots held 0.42 months of sales, about thirteen days. Dealers had almost nothing to sell. In 2025 the lots held about 1.4 months, still well below the old level.

Remember the smallest line on the census list? In 2022 America's car assemblers spent 2.9 billion dollars on semiconductors, about 1 per cent of what they bought. Yet a car cannot leave the line without its chips, any more than without its wheels. When the chip makers could not supply enough of them in 2021, carmakers had to stop their lines. General Motors told its investors that the shortage cost it more production in 2021 than the pandemic's shutdowns had in 2020. That was lean production's hidden bet: a system with no spare parts works beautifully until the part that is missing is one nobody thought about.
Suppliers: Chapter seven. The suppliers. If the carmaker buys most of the car, do its suppliers keep the money?

The carmaker sits at the top of a pyramid of suppliers. Below it are the tier-one suppliers, which sell finished systems straight to the carmaker: seats, wiring and electronics, drivetrains, airbags, whole sections of body. Below them, tier two and the makers of materials: chips, castings, foam, wire, glass, rubber. In America, the census of 2022 counted 170 companies assembling vehicles, with 213,363 employees, and 3,814 companies making parts, with 575,338. Most of the people who make cars do not work for carmakers.

What do the parts makers make? The census splits their shipments by kind. The biggest single branch is transmissions and the parts that carry power, about 66 billion dollars; then metal stampings, engines, seats and interiors, electrical and electronic equipment, steering and brakes. Each box is a business of its own, with its own customers and its own squeeze; and the engines, gearboxes and exhausts among them have no place in a battery car.

So do the suppliers keep the money the carmakers pay out? Over the eleven years to 2025, the large listed suppliers kept, on average, anything from a loss to about 9 cents of each dollar. Aptiv, the wiring and electronics maker, kept the most; Goodyear, the tyre maker, lost money on average. The carmakers did no better and no worse: General Motors 4.7 cents, Ford 2.5, Toyota 8.1. Everyone in this chain is thin. A carmaker buys each part from one of several possible suppliers and can move it to another at the next model; a supplier with a part nobody else can make, like a chip, has the upper hand, until someone else learns to make it. Few in the chain own something the buyer cannot get elsewhere.
Intermission: An intermission, and three lines from America's consumer price index, each set against all prices. Since 1948 prices in general have risen about 13 times. The price index for new vehicles has risen 4.7 times. Against everything else, a new car costs 0.35 of what it did, about a third, because the index counts the better car each year buys: the safety, the reliability, the electronics. Repairs went the other way. The price of having a car maintained and fixed rose 24 times, faster than prices in general. And used cars, after decades of drifting down, jumped 43 per cent between 2020 and 2022, when the chip shortage left the new car lots empty. Making cars is a business of falling prices. Fixing them is not.

And here is how many vehicles Americans bought each year since 1976, month by month. The line breathes with the economy. In a good year Americans buy around seventeen million. In the bad years they put off the purchase: 10.5 million a year in 1982, 10.6 million in 2009, and for one month in the spring of 2020, a rate of 8.9 million. A car is the easiest big purchase to postpone, because the old one still runs. Between 2007 and 2009 American sales fell by more than a third. So the business that needs its plants full sells a product whose demand can collapse in two years.
Dealers: Chapter eight. The dealer. How does a car dealer make its money, if not on new cars?

America's established carmakers sell through franchised dealers: independent businesses holding a franchise for a brand. AutoNation, one of the largest, owned 323 franchises in 245 stores at the end of 2025. Here is its revenue in 2025, by what it sold: almost half from new cars, more than a quarter from used cars, the rest from parts and service and from arranging loans and insurance. Now its gross profit. On a new car it kept only 4.9 per cent. On used cars, 5.9. But almost half of all its gross profit came from parts and service, fixing the cars it and others had sold, at a margin of 49 per cent. And almost a third came from finance and insurance: the commission for arranging the buyer's loan, the extended warranty, the service plan. The new car is the reason you walk in. The money is made after.

Even the thin margin on new cars moves with the shortage. In 2023, with lots still short of cars, AutoNation made 4,342 dollars of gross profit on each new car it sold. In 2025, 2,564. Dealers are a big business in their own right. In 2022 America had 17,242 new-car dealer companies with 22,483 dealerships, selling 1.2 trillion dollars' worth of cars, parts and service a year, and employing 1,150,441 people: more than the assembly plants and the parts makers together.

Why does the carmaker not sell to you directly and keep the dealer's share? Partly history: the established makers built their sales on independent dealers, who put up the money for the showrooms, the stock on the lots and the service bays. And partly law. Lucid's annual report explains that America's states license who may sell cars to their residents, and that some states do not let a carmaker be licensed as a dealer at all. The newcomers, Tesla, Rivian and Lucid, sell directly where the law allows, and Lucid's report warns that dealers may challenge it where the law is unclear. The established makers, with thousands of dealers under contract, cannot easily follow.
Finance: Chapter nine. A bank attached to a factory. Why does every big carmaker own a lender?

Many buyers borrow to buy a car, and the big carmakers own lenders to finance them. In 2025 GM Financial earned 2.8 billion dollars before tax, against 10.5 billion from building and selling cars in North America. Ford Credit earned 2.6 billion: almost as much as Ford's whole petrol car business, while its electric business lost nearly five. Toyota's lending arm made almost a quarter of its operating profit. And at Honda, in the year its car business lost one point four trillion yen, its financial services made a profit, and so, handsomely, did its motorcycles.

Why own a bank? Because to a buyer who borrows, the price of a car is a monthly payment. The rate on a four-year new-car loan from an American bank was above fifteen per cent in the early 1980s and around four to five through most of the 2010s; in 2026 it was 7.5. On a 52,075 dollar car with a tenth paid down, five years at that rate is about 938 dollars a month. When a carmaker wants to move cars without cutting the price on the window, its finance arm can offer a cheaper loan instead. The lender is a sales tool, and in good years a profitable one.

Leasing makes the bank part of the car business in another way. On a three-year lease the driver pays roughly what the car is expected to lose in value, plus interest. The lender keeps the rest: a car it must sell second-hand when the lease ends, at whatever used cars are fetching then. If used prices are ten per cent lower than it assumed, it loses about 3,020 dollars on every car. So the finance arm earns steadily in good times and carries the carmaker's risk again in bad ones, when car prices fall and more borrowers stop paying.
Profit: Chapter ten. Where the profit is. Which vehicles actually make money?

Start with what people buy. In America in 2025, only 16 per cent of new vehicles were cars in the old sense: saloons, hatchbacks, coupés. 56 per cent were crossovers, tall family vehicles somewhere between a car and an SUV, and 28 per cent were trucks: pickups and big sport utility vehicles. General Motors sold a third of all the trucks, and almost no cars, 2.1 per cent of that market. General Motors, with 17.2 per cent of the whole American market, has followed the money out of the car and into the truck.

Ford splits itself in three, and the split shows where the money is. Ford Blue sells petrol and hybrid cars to households: in 2025 it earned about 1,109 dollars on each vehicle. Ford Pro sells pickups and vans to businesses, fleets and governments, along with the servicing: about 4,599 dollars a vehicle, four times as much. And Ford Model e, its electric vehicles, lost about 27,000 dollars on each one it sold. Hold on to that number; it is the next chapter.

At the other extreme is luxury. Ferrari shipped 13,640 cars in 2025 and made 154,671 euros of operating profit on each. It keeps its volumes down on purpose, a 'controlled volume strategy', in its own words, to keep the brand exclusive. Toyota's car business made about 1,935 dollars on each of its 9.6 million. And the strangest number in the business: in the year to March 2026, Honda sold 14.7 million motorcycles and made 732 billion yen on them, while its car business, with 2.7 million cars, lost 1,411 billion. Same company, same brand; different business.
Electric: Chapter eleven. The electric car. What does the battery change, and why have so many lost money on it?

An electric car swaps the engine, gearbox, fuel tank and exhaust for a battery and a motor. The battery is the expensive part. America's Department of Energy estimates what a battery pack costs to make, per kilowatt-hour of energy it can store. In 2008, about 1,415 dollars in today's money. By 2023, 139: 90 per cent less. For a 75 kilowatt-hour pack, enough for a family car, that is the difference between 106,140 dollars and 10,425. If the engine, gearbox and exhaust it replaces cost something like 6,000 dollars to make, the battery reaches parity near 80 dollars a kilowatt-hour. Close, but not yet, by these estimates.

And so the share of electric cars has climbed, very unevenly. In Norway, 97 per cent of new cars sold in 2025 were electric. In China, 53 per cent: more than half. In Europe, 28; in the world as a whole, 25. In the United States, 10, and the federal tax credits for electric cars were repealed in 2025, as Tesla's own annual report notes. Much the same cars, and shares from one in ten to almost all: what differs from place to place is policy and price.

For the established makers, the electric car has so far been a way to lose money. Ford's electric business lost about 48,619 dollars per vehicle in 2024 and 27,000 in 2025, on sales too small to cover its costs. In 2025 the old makers wrote off a large part of their electric plans. Stellantis took charges of about 21 billion dollars, Ford 10.7 billion, General Motors 7.7 billion: platforms abandoned, programmes cancelled, battery plants resized. Tesla, which makes nothing but electric cars, does make money on them: its automotive gross margin was 17.8 per cent, and part of its revenue came from selling regulatory credits to other carmakers that needed them to meet emissions rules.
China: Chapter twelve. China. How did China come to export more cars than Japan?

Now the third arrival. These are the world's big car exporters, by the value of the passenger cars they ship abroad. Germany leads, then Japan; South Korea, Mexico and the United States follow. And this is China. In 2015 it exported 4 billion dollars' worth of cars. In 2020, 10. In 2025, 110 billion, more by value than Japan, and second only to Germany: 27 times as much in ten years.

The exports grew out of the biggest car market in the world. According to China's carmakers' association, China sold 34.4 million vehicles in 2025, and 48 per cent of them were what China calls new energy vehicles: battery cars and plug-in hybrids. BYD alone sold 4.6 million. But look at what it kept: 4.1 cents in the dollar, and its profit fell by a fifth. The foreign makers are losing ground: General Motors' share of China fell from 8.4 to 7.1 per cent in two years. Toyota's annual report describes China's market in four words: intense price competition. Many makers, each with plants to fill, each tempted to cut its price to fill them: it looks like the showroom duel from the start of this film, played on a national scale, and exports are one place for the extra cars to go.

The rest of the world has answered with tariffs. In September 2024 the United States raised its duty on electric cars from China to 100 per cent. A month later the European Union, after an investigation into Chinese subsidies, set extra duties maker by maker: 35.3 per cent for SAIC, 18.8 for Geely, 17.0 for BYD, and 7.8 for Tesla's Shanghai plant. Duties raise the price of a Chinese car abroad. They do not close the plants at home, so the pressure on prices stays in China, and in every market without a wall.
Labour: Chapter thirteen. Labour. What do the people on the line cost, and what does a strike cost?

The car has long been one of America's great employers. In 2000 about 1.3 million Americans worked making motor vehicles and their parts. By 2009, after the crash, 664 thousand: half the jobs gone in under a decade. They have come back part of the way, to about 967 thousand in 2025. And remember where they are: most in the parts makers, and more again selling and servicing cars at the dealers.

In September 2023 the United Auto Workers union went on strike at plants of General Motors, Ford and other makers. General Motors later estimated what the weeks of lost production cost it: about 1.1 billion dollars of North American operating profit. The new contract, which Ford says covers about 59,000 of its American workers, raised base wages by 11 per cent at once, 3 per cent in each of the next three Septembers and 5 per cent in 2027: 27 per cent in all, compounded. That sounds ruinous, but remember the dollar of chapter three: the assembly plants' payroll was under five cents of each dollar they shipped, so the raise adds about 1.3 cents. What made the strike expensive was not the wages. It was the idle plants, whose fixed costs ran on while nothing was built.
Landscape: Chapter fourteen. The landscape, as of November 2026. Who makes the world's cars, and who keeps anything?

Here is the industry as its accounts showed it in late 2026, each company placed by its revenue and by what it kept. The volume makers are huge and thin. Volkswagen and Toyota take in more than three hundred billion dollars a year each; Toyota kept about eight cents in the dollar, Volkswagen two, and Stellantis, Ford and Honda lost money. The Chinese makers: BYD, with about 112 billion dollars of revenue, kept 4 cents; the smaller electric makers listed in New York lost money or broke even. The electric newcomers in America: Tesla kept four cents, while Rivian lost 68 cents on every dollar and Lucid about twice its revenue, so far off this chart that they sit at its edge. The suppliers and the dealers mostly kept between one and seven cents; Goodyear lost money. And alone at the top, Ferrari: 22 cents in the dollar.

And the map of the business, by role. The volume makers, Japanese, German, Korean, American and French, each selling millions of cars a year. The luxury makers. The electric makers, most of them Chinese, with Tesla. India's own makers. The suppliers, including the battery makers, CATL and LG Energy Solution, which make the costliest part of an electric car. And the dealers and the lenders. Who keeps what has been the subject of the whole film.
Called: Chapter fifteen. Called it? What did people forecast about the electric car, and what happened?

This film's forecasts, starting with a carmaker's own. In May 2016 Tesla told its investors it would bring forward its plan to build half a million cars a year to 2018, two years earlier than planned. In 2018 it built 254,530: about half. In 2020 it built 509,737. The target was met on its original date, two years after the accelerated one: right about the destination, wrong about the time. New plants take years to reach their rate.

Next, America's Energy Information Administration, whose Annual Energy Outlook of January 2017 projected sales of every kind of light vehicle. Add up its battery and plug-in hybrid vehicles and it expected them to be 3.7 per cent of new vehicles in 2020 and 8.4 per cent in 2025. What happened: 2.3 per cent in 2020, 10 per cent in 2025. Too high early, too low late, and in the end not far off: a good forecast, as long-range forecasts go.

Now a government's plans. In April 2017 three Chinese ministries set targets for the car industry: two million new energy vehicles a year by 2020. China sold 1.37 million. Short. And by 2025, new energy vehicles above twenty per cent of sales. In 2025 they were 48 per cent. In 2020 the State Council restated the goal for 2025 as about twenty per cent. Five years out, the outcome was more than twice the plan.

And our own call. These are the IEA's figures for the electric share of new cars sold worldwide, 2015 to 2025. Fit the S-shaped curve that new technologies usually follow through the last five years, and it says 32 per cent in 2026. We think the real figure will come in below that: below 32 per cent, with a probability of 65 per cent. China, the biggest market, is already past half and has less room to grow; America repealed its tax credits in 2025; and the same curve already ran ahead of the actual figure for 2025. The IEA will publish the number in the middle of 2027, and we will score it here.
